title: Windows SQL Server Configuration Option Hunt
exclusions: Does not replace enterprise SIEM correlation for unrelated threat classes. Does not constitute legal, regulatory, or executive attestation for 'Windows SQL Server Configuration Option Hunt'. Does not cover entities explicitly scoped out in operational_exceptions.csv. Pair with sibling UCs in the same subcategory when the SPL surface alone cannot prove control effectiveness (see prerequisiteUseCases on UC-10.7.632).
evidence: Saved search uc_10_7_632_windows_sql_server_configuration_option, dashboard panel tied to this UC, weekly CSV export archived to index=evidence with change-ticket reference, and git-tracked lookup baselines referenced in the search.

controlTest.positiveScenario: On a lab host or staging index, ingest sample events that satisfy all SPL filters for 'Windows SQL Server Configuration Option Hunt'. Run the saved search manually and confirm at least one result row with populated severity or metric fields. Verify the alert action fires within one schedule interval and the output matches the dashboard table projection for UC-10.7.632.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Ingest a control batch where threshold fields remain within normal bounds (for example compliant configuration values, timestamps outside the monitoring window, or entities listed in operational_exceptions.csv). dataSources: Windows Event Log Application 15457 Collected via Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742) modular input or scripted poll into the index named in the SPL.
app: Splunk Security Essentials / ESCU — Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742)
spl:
`wineventlog_application` EventCode=15457
      | rex field=EventData_Xml "<Data>(?<config_name>[^<]+)</Data><Data>(?<old_value>[^<]+)</Data><Data>(?<new_value>[^<]+)</Data>"
      | rename host as dest
      | eval change_type=case( old_value="0" AND new_value="1", "enabled", old_value="1" AND new_value="0", "disabled", true(), "modified" )
      | eval risk_score=case( change_type="enabled", 90, change_type="disabled", 60, true(), 70 )
      | eval risk_message="SQL Server ".config_name." was ".change_type." on host ".dest
      | stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
        BY dest EventCode config_name
           change_type risk_message risk_score
      | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
      | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
      | `windows_sql_server_configuration_option_hunt_filter`
description: This detection helps hunt for changes to SQL Server configuration options that could indicate malicious activity. It monitors for modifications to any SQL Server configuration settings, allowing analysts to identify potentially suspicious changes that may be part of an attack, such as enabling dangerous features or modifying security-relevant settings.
value: Operations and leadership rely on 'Windows SQL Server Configuration Option Hunt' to catch regressions before they become customer-visible outages or audit findings. Early signal reduces mean time to repair, avoids duplicate manual log review, and preserves evidence for post-incident review without waiting for a user-reported ticket.
implementation: ESCU Hunting detection — not designed for automated alerting. Run ad-hoc or on a low-frequency schedule from Splunk Enterprise Security for analyst-driven investigation. Requires Windows Event Log Application 15457 ingested and CIM-normalized.
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable. No accelerated CIM datamodel tstats is implied by the main SPL; tune at the index and sourcetype level unless you add CIM normalization.
knownFalsePositives:
1. **Scheduled maintenance windows** — Planned change activity in the CMDB or change calendar produces expected deviations that match this detection pattern during approved maintenance. Cross-check ServiceNow change records for `state=implement` and the affected CI list.

2. **Backup and batch job cycles** — Nightly ETL, backup agents, or log rotation jobs generate bursts of similar events that resemble alert conditions but occur on a fixed schedule. Compare `_time` against the documented batch window before paging.

3. **Onboarding and provisioning bursts** — New users, devices, or services provisioned in bulk can temporarily skew counts until baselines stabilize. Filter events tagged `onboarding=true` in the identity or asset lookup.

4. **Monitoring and health-check traffic** — Synthetic transactions or internal scanner accounts generate probe traffic designed to exercise the control. Exclude service accounts listed in `monitoring_exceptions.csv`.

**Suppression mechanism:** Maintain a KV Store lookup `operational_exceptions.csv` with columns `entity`, `exception_reason`, `valid_from`, `valid_until`, and `approved_by`. Join the saved search to this lookup and filter `where isnull(exception_reason) OR now() > valid_until` so approved windows suppress alerts without muting the search globally.
detailedImplementation:
Enterprise Security Detection Rule

"Windows SQL Server Configuration Option Hunt" is a Hunting detection designed for analyst-driven threat hunting rather than automated alerting, sourced from the Splunk Enterprise Security Content Update (ESCU). Hunting detections are not intended for automated alerting. They are run on-demand or on a low-frequency schedule by security analysts investigating specific threat hypotheses.

Prerequisites

• Splunk Enterprise Security 7.x or later with the ES Content Update (ESCU) app installed and up to date.
• Data sources: Windows Event Log Application 15457. Must be ingested into Splunk and normalized to the Common Information Model (CIM) via the appropriate Technology Add-on.
• MITRE ATT&CK: T1505.001. Review the ATT&CK matrix for adjacent techniques to identify detection coverage gaps in your environment.

Deployment

1. In Enterprise Security, navigate to Configure → Content → Content Management.
2. Search for "Windows SQL Server Configuration Option Hunt" or filter by Analytic Story.
3. Hunting detections are typically left disabled for automated scheduling. Instead, run them on-demand from the Search bar or schedule at low frequency (daily or weekly).
4. Review results manually — hunting detections cast a wider net and expect analyst judgment to separate signal from noise.
5. When results warrant further investigation, create a Notable Event manually or initiate your incident response workflow.

Tuning and False Positive Management

Known false positives for this detection: Known-good admin tasks, change windows, and vendor agents can look suspicious out of context. Use scoped allowlists, asset context, and change-ticket checks before opening a high-severity incident.

• Hunting detections are expected to produce broader result sets that require analyst interpretation. Focus on refining the search scope (time range, specific hosts or users) rather than eliminating all noise.
• Maintain a hunting journal documenting hypotheses tested, results found, and detection improvements identified.
• Share high-fidelity findings with the detection engineering team to convert recurring hunting patterns into automated TTP or Anomaly detections.

Analyst Response Workflow

When reviewing Hunting results:

1. Run the search manually or review scheduled results. Evaluate each returned event against your threat hypothesis — not every result indicates compromise.
2. Cross-reference findings with current threat intelligence, recent security advisories, and outputs from other detection sources.
3. If suspicious activity is confirmed, create a Notable Event or escalate directly to your incident response process with the supporting evidence.
4. Document the hunting exercise: hypothesis, data sources queried, time range, findings, and any detection engineering improvements identified.

Validation

**Validate in production**

• Compare a sample of events with the source-of-truth console for the data source (cloud admin portal, device UI, or directory) covering the same time range.
• If you route findings through Enterprise Security, check the **Incident Review** queue and correlation search health so notables and drilldowns line up with what you see in search.

Step 1 — Configure data collection

Install and configure the add-on referenced in the app field (Splunk Security Essentials / ESCU — Splunk Add-on for Microsoft Windows (Splunkbase 742)). Enable the modular input or HEC token that writes sourcetype=see SPL into index=main. Default poll interval 300–900 seconds unless the vendor API rate-limits lower. Grant the ingestion role `list_inputs` and `search` on the target index.

Step 2 — Create the search and alert

Schedule the SPL with earliest=-24h@h and throttle per entity to avoid duplicate pages. Document tunable macros in the comment header. Understanding this SPL: filters in the first pipeline reduce license cost; stats/timechart aggregates define the alert grain; joins/lookups enrich owner or asset metadata for routing.

Step 3 — Validate

Compare `| tstats count where index=... sourcetype=...` against the vendor admin UI inventory count (+/-5%). Spot-check two known entities for field presence (`EventCode, change_type, config_name, dest`). Run `timechart count span=1h` over 7 days to find ingestion gaps longer than two poll intervals.

Step 4 — Operationalize

Add a dashboard row with single-value KPI tiles, a 24-hour timechart, and a drilldown table mirroring the SPL output columns. Route critical severity to the platform on-call channel; route warning to the service owner from the lookup.

Step 5 — Troubleshooting

No events: verify forwarder connectivity, HEC token ACLs, and that the modular input appears in `index=_internal source=*splunkd*`. NULL fields: check props/transforms order and TA version. Fewer results than expected: confirm index allow-lists on the search head role and that `_time` uses the correct timezone. API errors: inspect splunkd.log for HTTP 401/429 from the vendor endpoint configured in inputs.conf.
